notes.front: State Bayes' theorem and name the four parts.
notes.back:
P(H | E) = P(E | H) · P(H) / P(E)
Prior P(H): belief before evidence. Likelihood P(E|H): how expected the evidence is if H is true. Evidence / marginal P(E): how expected the evidence is overall. Posterior P(H|E): updated belief.Example: An alert fires (E). How likely is a real outage (H)? Depends on how often outages happen (prior), how reliably the alert fires during outages (likelihood), and how often the alert fires at all, including false alarms (evidence).

notes.front: Base-rate neglect: a test is 99% accurate for a disease that 1 in 10,000 people have. You test positive. Roughly how likely is it that you have the disease?
notes.back:
About 1%, not 99%.
Per 1,000,000 people: 100 have it → ~99 true positives. 999,900 don't → ~9,999 false positives. 99 / (99 + 9,999) ≈ 1%.
The prior (base rate) dominates when it is extreme.Example: An anomaly detector with a 1% false-positive rate on 100,000 daily requests produces ~1,000 false alarms a day. Even if it catches every real attack, most alerts are noise when real attacks are rare.

notes.front: What is a likelihood ratio, and how does it turn Bayes into a mental habit?
notes.back:
LR = P(E | H) / P(E | ¬H): how many times more likely the evidence is under H than under not-H.
In odds form: posterior odds = prior odds × LR. Evidence with LR ≈ 1 is uninformative no matter how dramatic it feels.Example: 'The service was deployed yesterday' as evidence for 'the deploy caused the incident': if deploys happen daily, P(deployed yesterday) is ~1 under both hypotheses, so LR ≈ 1 and it barely moves you.

notes.front: Why is 'extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence' just Bayes?
notes.back: A low prior needs a large likelihood ratio to reach a high posterior. Ordinary evidence (LR of 2–10) cannot lift a 1-in-a-million prior to anything credible.Example: A paper claims a 10× speedup from a trivial config change. Prior: such free wins are rare. You need strong, reproducible evidence, not one benchmark chart.

notes.front: Conditional probability P(A | B): what does it mean, and what is the classic confusion it invites?
notes.back: The probability of A restricted to the world where B is true. The confusion: P(A|B) ≠ P(B|A) (the 'prosecutor's fallacy').Example: P(error log contains 'timeout' | database is down) may be 95%. P(database is down | log contains 'timeout') may be 5%, because timeouts have many other causes.

notes.front: What does it mean for two events to be independent, and why does wrongly assuming it matter in engineering?
notes.back: P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B); knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Correlated failures break independence assumptions and make 'multiply the small probabilities' wildly optimistic.Example: Two disks each fail 1%/year. Independent: both fail ≈ 0.01%. But if they share a power supply, firmware bug, or rack, the joint probability can be closer to 1%. RAID math assumes independence that rarely holds.

notes.front: Define expected value and give the intuition for why it can mislead.
notes.back: E[X] = Σ x·P(x): the long-run average per trial. It is a summary, not a typical outcome—rare huge values dominate it.Example: A lottery ticket costs €2 and has expected value €1. Playing once, you almost surely lose €2. A service with mean latency 50 ms can have most requests at 10 ms and a few at 5 s.

notes.front: Variance and standard deviation: what do they measure, and why are units important?
notes.back: Variance = E[(X − μ)²], the average squared spread. Standard deviation σ = √variance, in the same units as X, so it is interpretable.Example: Two API endpoints both average 100 ms. One has σ = 5 ms (predictable), the other σ = 200 ms (a lottery). Same mean, completely different user experience and capacity needs.

notes.front: What does the Law of Large Numbers say, and what does it NOT say?
notes.back: The sample average converges to the true mean as n grows. It does not say deviations 'even out' in the short run (the gambler's fallacy), nor say anything about how fast convergence happens for heavy-tailed data.Example: After 10 heads in a row, the next flip is still 50/50. The average tends to 0.5 by drowning the 10 heads in thousands of later flips, not by producing extra tails.

notes.front: What does the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) say, and what is its main practical consequence?
notes.back: The sum (or mean) of many independent, finite-variance random variables is approximately normal, regardless of the individual distributions. Consequence: means of samples are well-behaved, so confidence intervals on averages work even when the underlying data is skewed.Example: Individual request latencies are lumpy and skewed. The daily average latency across a million requests is nearly normal, so you can put an error bar on it. But the CLT needs finite variance—it silently fails for power-law data.

notes.front: Bernoulli and Binomial distributions: what do they model?
notes.back: Bernoulli: one yes/no trial with success probability p. Binomial(n, p): number of successes in n independent trials. Mean np, variance np(1−p).Example: Each of 500 hosts has a 2% chance of failing a health check. Failures ~ Binomial(500, 0.02): mean 10, σ ≈ 3.1. Seeing 25 failures is ~5σ—something systemic is happening.

notes.front: Poisson distribution: what does it model, and what is its key property?
notes.back: Counts of independent events in a fixed interval when events occur at a constant average rate λ. Mean = variance = λ. Good default for arrivals, errors, and defects.Example: A service gets 100 requests/s on average. In any given second, P(≥130 requests) ≈ 0.2%—so a fixed capacity of 130 rps will be exceeded in roughly 1 second out of every 500, even with no traffic spike.

notes.front: Exponential distribution and the memoryless property: what do they mean?
notes.back: Exponential(λ) models time between Poisson events; mean 1/λ. Memoryless: P(wait > s+t | already waited s) = P(wait > t). The past waiting time gives no information.Example: If bus arrivals were truly Poisson, having waited 20 minutes already would not make the bus 'due'. Real buses are scheduled, so they are not memoryless; radioactive decay and many failure processes are.

notes.front: Normal (Gaussian) distribution: when is it a reasonable model and when is it a trap?
notes.back: Reasonable when the quantity is a sum of many small independent effects (heights, measurement noise, sample means). A trap for anything bounded at zero, multiplicative, or driven by rare large events: latency, income, file sizes, outage cost.Example: Modeling latency as normal with mean 100 ms and σ 50 ms implies negative latencies and a p99.9 of ~250 ms. Real p99.9 might be 3 s.

notes.front: Log-normal distribution: what generates it, and how do you recognize it?
notes.back: If X = product of many positive random factors, log X is a sum, so log X is normal. Recognize it by right skew with a long tail and a histogram that looks normal on a log axis. Common for latency, response sizes, incomes, city sizes.Example: Request latency = network × queueing × DB × serialization, each a multiplicative slowdown. The result is log-normal-ish: median 40 ms, mean 70 ms, p99 500 ms.

notes.front: Heavy-tailed / power-law distributions: what is different about them, and why does the mean become useless?
notes.back: P(X > x) decays polynomially, not exponentially, so extremes are not rare enough to ignore. The sample mean is dominated by the largest observation and may not converge; variance can be infinite.Example: Cascading-failure cost, file sizes on a shared drive, follower counts. 'Average outage cost' is meaningless when one outage per decade dwarfs all others combined. Plan for the tail, not the mean.

notes.front: Why report percentiles (p50, p99) instead of the mean, and what does 'p99 at scale' imply?
notes.back: Percentiles describe the distribution's shape; the mean hides tails. At scale, a user's page fans out to many backend calls, so the user sees the backend's tail on nearly every request.Example: If a page calls 100 services each with a p99 of 1 s, the chance that at least one call is slow is 1 − 0.99100 ≈ 63%. The backend p99 becomes the user's p37.

notes.front: What is a null hypothesis, and what does a hypothesis test actually do?
notes.back: H₀ is the 'nothing interesting is happening' model (no difference, no effect). A test asks: if H₀ were true, how surprising would data this extreme be? It never proves H₀; it can only fail to reject it.Example: A/B test: H₀ = new checkout flow converts the same as old. You observe +2%. The test asks how often random noise alone would produce +2% or more.

notes.front: Define the p-value precisely and state the most common misreading.
notes.back: p = P(data at least this extreme | H₀ true). It is NOT P(H₀ | data), and 1 − p is NOT the probability the effect is real.Example: p = 0.03 for 'new caching layer reduced latency'. It means: if caching did nothing, a gap this large would appear by chance 3% of the time. Whether caching really helps also depends on the prior plausibility and effect size.

notes.front: Type I vs Type II error, and why you cannot minimize both for free.
notes.back: Type I (false positive): rejecting a true H₀. Type II (false negative): failing to reject a false H₀. Tightening the threshold for one loosens the other; only more data (or a better test) improves both.Example: Paging threshold: alert on any latency bump → many false pages (Type I). Alert only on huge bumps → missed slow-burn degradations (Type II).

notes.front: What is statistical power, and what is the practical failure that comes from ignoring it?
notes.back: Power = P(reject H₀ | effect is real) = 1 − Type II rate. Underpowered studies mostly miss real effects, and the effects they do 'find' are inflated (the winner's curse).Example: You A/B test with 200 users to detect a 1% conversion lift. Power is ~5%. A null result means nothing, and a 'significant' result is almost certainly a fluke that overstates the true effect.

notes.front: What does a 95% confidence interval mean, and what does it not mean?
notes.back: Procedure-level guarantee: if you repeated the experiment many times, 95% of the intervals built this way would contain the true value. It does not mean 'there is a 95% probability the true value is in this particular interval' (that is a Bayesian credible interval).Example: 'Error rate 0.4% (95% CI 0.1%–0.9%)' tells you the data is compatible with anything from 0.1% to 0.9%. A point estimate without an interval hides that the true value could be 9× higher.

notes.front: The multiple-comparisons problem: what is it and how do you spot it?
notes.back: Test enough hypotheses and some will hit p < 0.05 by chance (5% of true nulls, on average). Spot it: many metrics, subgroups, or time windows checked; only the winners reported. Fixes: Bonferroni, false-discovery-rate control, pre-registration.Example: A dashboard with 40 metrics. After a deploy, one metric is 'significantly' worse at p < 0.05. Expected number of such false alarms with no real change: 2.

notes.front: What is p-hacking / the garden of forking paths?
notes.back: Making analysis choices (which outliers to drop, which metric, when to stop collecting) after seeing the data, so that some path reaches significance. Each choice is defensible; the combination guarantees a 'finding'.Example: An A/B test is 'not significant yet' at day 7, so you run it to day 12 and stop the moment it crosses p = 0.05. Peeking like this inflates the false-positive rate to 20–30%.

notes.front: Statistical significance vs practical significance (effect size).
notes.back: With enough data, trivially small effects become 'significant'. Always ask: how big is the effect, with what interval, and does that size matter?Example: A change improves p50 latency by 0.3 ms, p < 0.0001, measured on 50 million requests. Significant and irrelevant.

notes.front: Regression to the mean: what is it and what does it fool people into believing?
notes.back: Extreme measurements are partly luck; the next measurement will be closer to average even if nothing changed. It fools people into crediting whatever intervention followed the extreme.Example: You fix the three worst-performing services after a bad week. Next week they improve. Regression to the mean predicts most of that improvement with no fix at all.

notes.front: Simpson's paradox: describe it with an example.
notes.back: A trend present in every subgroup reverses when the groups are combined, because group sizes differ across the comparison.Example: Cluster A has a lower error rate than cluster B for both small requests and large requests. Yet A's overall error rate is higher, because A handles mostly large (error-prone) requests. Aggregates without stratification lie.

notes.front: Correlation vs causation: list the three main explanations for an observed correlation between X and Y.
notes.back: (1) X causes Y. (2) Y causes X (reverse causation). (3) Z causes both (confounding). Plus: chance, and selection effects in how the data was collected.Example: Services with more monitoring have more incidents. Monitoring causes incidents? No: important services get both more monitoring and more scrutiny (confounder), and incidents lead to more monitoring (reverse).

notes.front: What is a confounder, and how does randomization deal with it?
notes.back: A variable that influences both the treatment and the outcome, creating a spurious association. Randomizing treatment breaks the confounder's link to treatment, so any remaining outcome difference is causal (in expectation).Example: Users who enable dark mode retain better. Confounder: engaged power users both enable dark mode and retain. Randomly forcing dark mode on for half of new users removes that link.

notes.front: What is a collider, and why can conditioning on one create a fake correlation (Berkson's paradox)?
notes.back: A collider is a variable caused by both X and Y. Selecting or conditioning on it induces a correlation between X and Y that does not exist in the population.Example: Among hired candidates, coding-test score and interview charm are negatively correlated—because hiring required being strong in at least one. In the applicant pool they are unrelated.

notes.front: Selection bias and survivorship bias: describe and give the canonical example.
notes.back: Selection bias: the sample is not representative because of how it was chosen. Survivorship bias: you only see cases that made it through some filter.Example: WWII bombers returned with bullet holes on wings and fuselage; the fix was to armor the engines—the places with no holes, because planes hit there never came back. Postmortems only cover incidents that got noticed.

notes.front: What is the counterfactual definition of a causal effect, and why is it unobservable?
notes.back: Effect of X on unit i = Yi(X = 1) − Yi(X = 0). Only one of the two outcomes ever happens (the fundamental problem of causal inference). All causal methods are ways of estimating the missing one.Example: Did the migration reduce cost? The counterfactual is the cost this quarter had you not migrated—which you never observe. Comparing to last quarter assumes nothing else changed.

notes.front: Name three quasi-experimental methods for causal inference without randomization and the assumption each relies on.
notes.back: Difference-in-differences: treated and control groups would have moved in parallel absent treatment. Instrumental variable: something nudges treatment but affects the outcome only through treatment. Regression discontinuity: units just above and just below a cutoff are comparable.Example: Diff-in-diff: region EU got the new autoscaler, US did not. Compare EU's before/after change to US's before/after change, which nets out the global traffic trend.

notes.front: Why does 'we changed X and metric Y improved' prove little, and what would strengthen it?
notes.back: Time-based before/after comparisons are confounded by everything else that changed (traffic, other deploys, seasonality) and by regression to the mean. Strengthen with a concurrent control, randomization, a dose-response pattern, or a mechanism plus a reversal test (turn it off, does Y degrade?).Example: Latency improved after the JVM flag change—during the weekend traffic dip. Turn the flag off on half the fleet on Monday and compare.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: State Little's Law and its three variables.
notes.back:
L = λ · W
L = average number of items in the system, λ = average arrival (= throughput) rate, W = average time an item spends in the system. Holds for any stable system, regardless of arrival or service distribution.Example: A coffee shop serves 60 customers/hour and each spends 10 minutes inside → on average 60 × (1/6) = 10 customers in the shop.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: Use Little's Law to size a thread pool or connection pool.
notes.back: Concurrency needed = throughput × latency. L = λW with λ in requests/s and W in seconds.Example: 1,000 rps with 50 ms average latency → 1000 × 0.05 = 50 concurrent requests in flight. A pool of 40 will queue; a pool of 500 wastes memory. If latency doubles under a DB slowdown, needed concurrency doubles too—which is how pools exhaust in cascades.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: Use Little's Law to infer something you cannot measure directly.
notes.back: Any one of L, λ, W can be derived from the other two.Example: A Kafka consumer group has a stable backlog of 200,000 messages and processes 5,000 msg/s → each message waits 200000/5000 = 40 s in the queue, even though no message is timestamped. Similarly: 30 open tickets, 5 closed/week → 6 weeks average cycle time.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: What is utilization ρ, and what is the crucial nonlinearity in the relation between utilization and waiting time?
notes.back: ρ = λ / μ (arrival rate / service rate). Waiting time grows roughly as ρ / (1 − ρ): flat when ρ is low, then explodes near 1. Going from 50% to 90% utilization multiplies wait ~9×; 90% to 99% another ~10×.Example: A CPU at 95% utilization looks 'efficiently used' on a dashboard and is a latency disaster: each request waits behind ~19 others on average.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: For an M/M/1 queue, what are the formulas for average number in system and average time in system?
notes.back: L = ρ / (1 − ρ), W = 1 / (μ − λ). Service time S = 1/μ, so W = S / (1 − ρ).Example: Service time 10 ms (μ = 100/s), arrivals 80/s → ρ = 0.8, W = 10 / 0.2 = 50 ms. Push arrivals to 95/s → W = 200 ms. Add 19% load, get 4× latency.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: What does Kendall notation A/S/c mean? Decode M/M/1 and M/G/k.
notes.back: A = arrival process, S = service-time distribution, c = number of servers. M = Markovian (Poisson arrivals / exponential service), G = general, D = deterministic. M/M/1: Poisson arrivals, exponential service, one server. M/G/k: Poisson arrivals, arbitrary service distribution, k servers.Example: A single-threaded worker with Poisson request arrivals and wildly varying job sizes is M/G/1—and the 'G' is where the pain lives.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: Kingman's formula: what does it say about the effect of variability on queueing delay?
notes.back: Wq ≈ (ρ / (1 − ρ)) · ((ca² + cs²) / 2) · S, where ca, cs are the coefficients of variation of inter-arrival and service times. Delay scales with variability squared: burstiness and uneven job sizes hurt as much as load does.Example: Two systems at 80% utilization. One has uniform 10 ms jobs; the other mixes 1 ms and 500 ms jobs. The second has far worse queueing delay at the same utilization. Splitting big jobs or isolating them into their own queue reduces cs.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: Why do Poisson arrivals make bursts inevitable even at constant average load?
notes.back: Poisson processes are maximally random: for rate λ per interval, the count has variance λ, so intervals with 2–3× the average load occur routinely. Capacity planned at the average will queue constantly.Example: Average 10 requests per 100 ms window. P(≥ 20 in a window) ≈ 0.3%, i.e. ~30 times a second-long burst per ~10 s of traffic. Buffers and headroom exist to absorb this, not for 'spikes'.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: One shared queue with k servers vs k separate queues (one per server): which is better and why?
notes.back: One shared queue (M/M/k) is strictly better: no server idles while another has a backlog, and a single slow job blocks only one server, not a whole line. Separate queues suffer from imbalance and head-of-line blocking.Example: Supermarket with one snake line feeding 6 tills vs 6 independent lines: the snake line has lower average wait. Same reason a single work queue with a worker pool beats per-worker queues, and why round-robin load balancing to fixed-size per-instance queues is worse than least-loaded routing.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: What is head-of-line blocking, and where does it show up?
notes.back: A slow item at the front of a FIFO queue delays everything behind it, even items that could be served instantly. Shows up in TCP (one lost packet stalls the stream), HTTP/1.1 pipelining, single-threaded event loops, and per-partition ordered consumers.Example: A Kafka partition consumed in order: one message that triggers a 30 s external call delays the 10,000 messages behind it by 30 s. Solutions: per-key ordering with parallelism across keys, or moving slow work off the critical path.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: Why does an overloaded system's throughput often collapse rather than plateau (the 'thrashing' or congestion collapse pattern)?
notes.back: Queued work still consumes resources (memory, retries, timeouts, context switches), so past saturation, effective service rate μ decreases while λ stays high. Clients time out and retry, adding load. Useful throughput falls below what the system could do at moderate load.Example: A DB at 100% CPU: queries time out at 30 s, clients retry, now each query costs 3 attempts. Fix: load shedding, backpressure, bounded queues, and retry budgets—drop work early so the rest completes.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: What is the Universal Scalability Law (USL), and what two effects does it add to Amdahl's Law?
notes.back: Throughput(N) = N / (1 + α(N − 1) + βN(N − 1)). α = contention (serialized portion, Amdahl), β = coherency cost (cross-talk: cache invalidation, locks, consensus). With β > 0 throughput peaks and then falls as you add nodes.Example: Adding replicas to a strongly consistent database: at first throughput rises, then coordination overhead (β) dominates and adding the 12th node makes everything slower.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Queueing Theory & Little's Law
notes.front: Tail latency amplification under fan-out: how do you compute it, and what are the mitigations?
notes.back: P(at least one of N calls is slow) = 1 − (1 − p)N. Mitigations: hedged requests (send a duplicate after the p95 delay), tied requests, limiting fan-out, deadline propagation, and reducing variance in the backend rather than the mean.Example: N = 20 backends, each with p = 1% slow: 1 − 0.9920 ≈ 18% of user requests are slow. Hedging the slowest 5% cuts user-visible tail dramatically for ~5% extra load.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: What is a vector, in the sense used in ML papers?
notes.back: An ordered list of numbers representing a point or direction in n-dimensional space. In ML, almost everything is a vector: a word embedding, an image's pixels, a user's feature row, the parameters of a model.Example: A user = [age, sessions/week, avg order value] = [34, 3, 42.5] is a point in ℝ³. An embedding of the word 'queue' might be 768 numbers describing its meaning.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Dot product: formula and geometric meaning. Why is it everywhere in ML?
notes.back: a·b = Σ aibi = |a||b| cos θ. It measures alignment: large when vectors point the same way, zero when orthogonal, negative when opposed. Every neuron computes a dot product of inputs with weights; attention scores are dot products of queries and keys.Example: Cosine similarity = dot product of unit vectors. Two document embeddings with cosine 0.92 are about the same topic; 0.05 means unrelated. Semantic search is 'find the vectors with the largest dot product with the query'.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: What is a matrix, and what does multiplying a vector by a matrix do?
notes.back: A matrix is a linear map: it takes a vector and returns a vector, via rotation, scaling, shearing, or projection, but never bending. Ax combines the columns of A using the entries of x as weights.Example: A 2×2 matrix [[2,0],[0,1]] stretches the x-axis by 2. A rotation matrix turns every vector by the same angle. A neural-network layer y = Wx + b is a linear map followed by a shift.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Why is matrix multiplication defined the way it is, and what does AB mean?
notes.back: AB is the composition 'apply B, then A'. The definition is exactly what makes (AB)x = A(Bx). Inner dimensions must match because B's output must fit A's input. Not commutative: rotate-then-stretch ≠ stretch-then-rotate.Example: A deep network with no nonlinearities, W₃W₂W₁x, collapses to a single matrix W = W₃W₂W₁: stacking linear layers gains nothing. Nonlinear activations between layers are what make depth matter.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Transpose, identity, and inverse: what does each do?
notes.back: Transpose Aᵀ swaps rows and columns (turns 'weights applied to inputs' into 'inputs applied to weights'; xᵀy is the dot product). Identity I leaves vectors unchanged. Inverse A⁻¹ undoes A; it exists only if A loses no information (square and full rank).Example: A projection onto a plane has no inverse: once you flatten a 3D point to 2D, you cannot recover the height. Solving Ax = b for x is 'undo A', which is why singular A means no unique solution.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Rank of a matrix: what is it intuitively, and why do papers talk about 'low-rank'?
notes.back: Rank = number of independent directions the matrix's output can span = the true dimensionality of what it does. Low rank means the matrix is 'mostly redundant' and can be written as a product of two thin matrices.Example: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) fine-tunes a model by learning ΔW = AB where A is d×8 and B is 8×d instead of the full d×d update: 1,000× fewer parameters, on the bet that the needed change is low-rank.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: definition and intuition.
notes.back: Av = λv: v is a direction the matrix only stretches (by λ), never rotates. Eigenvectors are the 'natural axes' of a linear map; eigenvalues say how much each axis is amplified or damped.Example: PageRank is the leading eigenvector of the web's link matrix: the ranking that is unchanged when you 'flow' importance along links once more. Repeatedly applying a matrix amplifies the direction with the largest |λ|—that is the power iteration algorithm.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: What does Principal Component Analysis (PCA) do, and how does it relate to eigenvectors?
notes.back: Finds the orthogonal directions of maximum variance in data. They are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix; the eigenvalues are the variance along each. Keeping the top k gives the best k-dimensional linear approximation.Example: 50 server metrics are collected, but most co-move with load. PCA might show 2 components explain 90% of the variance: 'overall load' and 'disk vs CPU bound'. Plot those 2 instead of 50 dashboards.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD): what is it and why is it the workhorse?
notes.back: Any matrix A = UΣVᵀ: rotate (Vᵀ), scale along axes (Σ, the singular values), rotate (U). Works for non-square matrices. Truncating small singular values gives the best low-rank approximation (Eckart–Young).Example: A 10,000 users × 5,000 items rating matrix, mostly empty. Keep the top 50 singular values: each user and item becomes a 50-dim vector, and their dot product predicts missing ratings. That is a recommender system.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: L1 norm vs L2 norm: definitions and the geometric difference that matters for ML.
notes.back: L2 (Euclidean): √Σxi², a ball. L1 (Manhattan): Σ|xi|, a diamond with corners on the axes. Penalizing L1 pushes weights exactly to zero (sparse); penalizing L2 shrinks them smoothly toward zero.Example: Lasso regression (L1) on 200 features selects 12 and zeroes the rest—an interpretable model. Ridge (L2) keeps all 200 small. The diamond's corners touch the loss contours where coordinates are zero.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Softmax: formula and what it does.
notes.back: softmax(z)i = ezi / Σj ezj. Turns arbitrary real scores into a probability distribution, exaggerating differences: the largest score gets most of the mass. Dividing z by a 'temperature' T sharpens (T→0) or flattens (T→∞) it.Example: Logits [2, 1, 0] → probabilities [0.67, 0.24, 0.09]. At temperature 0.1, → [0.9999, ...]: greedy. At temperature 10, nearly uniform. LLM sampling temperature is exactly this knob.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Derivative: what does dy/dx tell you, in plain language?
notes.back: The sensitivity of y to a tiny change in x: 'if I nudge x by ε, y moves by about (dy/dx)·ε'. It is the slope of the local linear approximation.Example: Loss as a function of a weight: d(loss)/d(w) = −3 means increasing w slightly decreases loss about 3× as fast. So move w up. That single sentence is gradient descent.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Partial derivatives and the gradient: definitions and the key geometric fact.
notes.back: ∂f/∂xi: sensitivity to one variable, others held fixed. Gradient ∇f = vector of all partials. Key fact: ∇f points in the direction of steepest ascent, and its magnitude is the slope in that direction. Steepest descent is −∇f.Example: Standing on a hillside blindfolded: the gradient is the direction your feet feel the ground rising fastest. Walking downhill by feel, one small step at a time, is gradient descent on the terrain.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Chain rule: statement and why it is the whole of backpropagation.
notes.back: If y = f(g(x)), then dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x): sensitivities multiply along a chain. A neural network is a long chain of functions, so the gradient of the loss with respect to any early weight is a product of local derivatives along the path from that weight to the loss.Example: Loss ← output ← layer 3 ← layer 2 ← layer 1 ← w. Backprop computes ∂loss/∂w by multiplying five local Jacobians from the loss backward, reusing intermediate products for all weights. If each factor is < 1, the product vanishes (the vanishing gradient problem).

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Jacobian and Hessian: what are they and when do you meet them?
notes.back: Jacobian: the matrix of all first partials of a vector-valued function (the best linear approximation of f: ℝⁿ→ℝᵐ). Hessian: the matrix of second partials of a scalar function; it describes curvature. Backprop multiplies Jacobians; second-order optimizers (Newton) use the Hessian.Example: The Hessian's eigenvalues tell you whether a point is a minimum (all positive), maximum (all negative), or saddle (mixed). A 'sharp' minimum has large eigenvalues and is said to generalize worse than a 'flat' one.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Convexity: what is a convex function, and why do ML people care?
notes.back: A function whose graph lies below any chord (bowl-shaped): any local minimum is the global minimum, so gradient descent is guaranteed to find the best answer. Linear and logistic regression have convex losses; deep networks do not.Example: A convex loss is a valley: roll a ball anywhere and it ends at the bottom. A non-convex loss is a mountain range: where you start and how you step determines which valley you land in. That is why random seeds change deep-learning results.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Integral: what is it, and how does it show up in probability?
notes.back: The accumulated total of a quantity over an interval (area under the curve). In probability, P(a < X < b) = ∫ab p(x) dx and E[g(X)] = ∫ g(x) p(x) dx: integrating a density over a region gives probability; integrating a value times density gives an average.Example: The mean of an exponential distribution with rate λ is ∫₀^∞ x·λe−λx dx = 1/λ. A marginal likelihood P(E) = ∫ P(E|θ)P(θ) dθ 'sums over all possible parameter values, weighted by how plausible each is'.

notes.deck: Quantitative Foundations for Engineers::Linear Algebra & Calculus
notes.front: Taylor expansion: what is it and why does it appear in optimization?
notes.back: Approximating f near a point using its derivatives: f(x+δ) ≈ f(x) + f′(x)δ + ½f″(x)δ² + … First-order term justifies gradient descent (small steps along −∇f decrease f). Second-order term (Hessian) justifies Newton's method and explains why too large a learning rate overshoots.Example: Loss ≈ L(w) + g·δ + ½δᵀHδ. If the step δ = −ηg is so big that the ½δᵀHδ curvature term outweighs the g·δ gain, loss goes up instead of down—the 'learning rate too high' divergence.

notes.front: What is one bit of information, in Shannon's sense?
notes.back: The amount of information that halves your uncertainty: the answer to one fair yes/no question. An event of probability p carries −log₂ p bits of 'surprise'.Example: Learning a fair coin landed heads: 1 bit. Learning a die showed 4: log₂ 6 ≈ 2.58 bits. Learning the sun rose: ≈ 0 bits, you already knew. A 1-in-a-million event: ~20 bits.

notes.front: Define entropy H(X) and give its intuition.
notes.back: H(X) = −Σ p(x) log₂ p(x): the average surprise per outcome, i.e. how unpredictable the source is. Maximal for a uniform distribution, zero for a certain outcome.Example: Fair coin: 1 bit. Coin that lands heads 99% of the time: 0.08 bits—almost nothing to learn from each flip. A log line that is always 'OK' has zero entropy; a log with rich variety has high entropy.

notes.front: Shannon's source-coding theorem: what does entropy have to do with compression?
notes.back: Entropy is the minimum average number of bits per symbol any lossless code can achieve. You cannot compress below entropy; you can get arbitrarily close. Compression = assigning short codes to likely symbols.Example: English text has ~1–1.5 bits of entropy per character but is stored at 8 bits/char. That ~6× redundancy is what gzip exploits. A file of random bytes has 8 bits/byte entropy: gzip cannot shrink it, and 'compressing' it makes it slightly larger.

notes.front: Huffman coding: the idea in one sentence, and the intuition it makes concrete.
notes.back: Build a binary tree by repeatedly merging the two least-probable symbols; frequent symbols end up near the root with short codes. Makes concrete: optimal code length for symbol x is ≈ −log₂ p(x).Example: Morse code is a hand-made version: 'E' (most common letter) is a single dot; 'Q' is dash-dash-dot-dash.

notes.front: Cross-entropy H(p, q): definition and why it is the standard ML loss.
notes.back: H(p, q) = −Σ p(x) log q(x): the average bits needed to encode data from true distribution p using a code optimized for q. Minimized when q = p. Training a classifier to minimize cross-entropy = making the model's predicted distribution match the true one.Example: True label is 'cat' (p = [1, 0]). Model says [0.9, 0.1] → loss = −log 0.9 ≈ 0.15. Model says [0.1, 0.9] → −log 0.1 ≈ 3.3. Confident wrong answers are punished exponentially harder than unsure ones.

notes.front: Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence: definition, intuition, and two properties.
notes.back: DKL(p ‖ q) = Σ p(x) log(p(x)/q(x)) = H(p,q) − H(p): the extra bits wasted by encoding p-data with a q-optimized code; how much a model q misses about reality p. Properties: always ≥ 0; not symmetric (D(p‖q) ≠ D(q‖p)).Example: Reinforcement learning from human feedback keeps a KL penalty between the tuned model and the base model: 'improve on the reward but don't drift more than a few bits per token from what you were'.

notes.front: Mutual information I(X; Y): what does it measure and how is it better than correlation?
notes.back: I(X;Y) = H(X) − H(X | Y): how many bits knowing Y tells you about X. Zero iff independent. Unlike correlation, it captures any dependence (nonlinear, non-monotonic, categorical).Example: Y = X² for X in [−1, 1] has correlation 0 but high mutual information. Feature selection by mutual information catches features correlation-based filters miss.

notes.front: Perplexity: what is it and how do you read a language model's perplexity?
notes.back: Perplexity = 2cross-entropy (bits) = ecross-entropy (nats): the effective number of equally likely choices the model is 'confused between' per token.Example: Perplexity 20 on a test set means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if it were picking uniformly among 20 tokens. A model with perplexity 10 has compressed the language twice as tightly.

notes.front: 'Compression is prediction': explain the equivalence.
notes.back: A predictor that assigns probability q(x) to the next symbol can encode it in −log₂ q(x) bits (arithmetic coding), and any compressor implicitly defines a predictor. Better prediction ⇔ shorter encoding. Training an LLM by minimizing cross-entropy is literally building a compressor for text.Example: A trained LLM compresses text far better than gzip because it 'knows' that after 'the capital of France is' the next token is nearly certain. Its loss in bits/token is exactly its compression rate.

notes.front: Why is randomness incompressible, and what does that tell you about detecting structure?
notes.back: A truly random sequence has no shorter description than itself (Kolmogorov complexity ≈ length). Compressibility is therefore a test for structure: if gzip shrinks it, there is a pattern.Example: Encrypted or compressed data looks random: a 1 GB file that gzip cannot shrink is either already compressed, encrypted, or noise. Conversely, if 'random' session IDs compress noticeably, the generator is flawed.

notes.front: Channel capacity and the noisy-channel coding theorem: what do they say?
notes.back: Every noisy channel has a capacity C (bits/use). Below rate C you can transmit with arbitrarily low error using clever error-correcting codes; above C you cannot. Reliability comes from redundancy structured cleverly, not from shouting louder.Example: Shannon–Hartley: C = B log₂(1 + SNR). Doubling bandwidth doubles capacity; doubling signal power adds only ~1 bit per Hz. This is why Wi-Fi gets faster with wider channels rather than more power.

notes.front: Maximum-entropy principle: what does it say, and why is the normal distribution special?
notes.back: Among all distributions consistent with what you know (constraints), pick the one with the highest entropy: it assumes nothing extra. Known mean and variance → Gaussian. Known mean of a positive quantity → exponential. Known support only → uniform.Example: If all you know about latency is its mean, the least-assuming model is exponential. Modeling it as Gaussian smuggles in a claim (symmetry, thin tails) you have no evidence for.

notes.front: Entropy as a measure of password or key strength: how do you compute it and what is the trap?
notes.back: Bits = log₂(number of equally likely possibilities the attacker must search). Trap: entropy is a property of the generating process, not the string. A human-chosen 'complex' password has far less entropy than its length suggests because humans pick from a tiny, predictable set.Example: 4 random words from a 7,776-word list: log₂(7776⁴) ≈ 51.7 bits. 'P@ssw0rd2024!' looks complex but is in every cracking dictionary: a few bits. 128-bit key: 2¹²⁸ tries ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸.

notes.front: Minimum Description Length (MDL) / Occam's razor via information theory.
notes.back: The best model is the one that minimizes (bits to describe the model) + (bits to describe the data given the model). A model that fits perfectly but is enormous has not explained anything; a tiny model with small residuals has.Example: A 200-parameter polynomial through 200 points has zero error but costs 200 numbers to state: it has memorized, not compressed. A line with small noise costs 2 numbers plus cheap residuals—that is the real pattern.

notes.front: What is a loss function, and what is the relationship between loss and what you actually care about?
notes.back: A differentiable number that measures how wrong the model is on training data; training minimizes it. It is a proxy: you optimize cross-entropy or squared error because you can, not because it is the business metric. The gap between proxy and goal is where models 'game' the objective.Example: Optimizing click-through rate as a proxy for 'user value' produces clickbait. Optimizing squared error on house prices lets a few mansions dominate the fit.

notes.front: Gradient descent: the algorithm in one line, and what the learning rate does.
notes.back: w ← w − η ∇L(w): repeatedly step against the gradient. η (learning rate) is step size. Too small: crawls, may stall. Too large: overshoots the valley, oscillates or diverges.Example: Walking downhill in fog: tiny steps take forever; giant leaps jump across the valley to the opposite slope. Learning-rate schedules start big to move fast and shrink to settle.

notes.front: Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and mini-batches: why not compute the exact gradient?
notes.back: The full-dataset gradient costs one pass over all data per step. SGD estimates it from a small random batch: noisy but ~1,000× cheaper, so you take far more steps. The noise also helps escape sharp minima and saddle points.Example: Polling 1,000 voters gives a good estimate of the national mood at a fraction of the cost of asking everyone. Batch size trades gradient accuracy against steps per second.

notes.front: Overfitting: definition and how you detect it.
notes.back: The model learns noise and idiosyncrasies of the training data instead of the underlying pattern; training error keeps falling while held-out error rises. Detect it with a validation set you never train on.Example: A student who memorizes last year's exam answers scores 100% on that exam and fails a new one. A fraud model that learns 'transactions on 2024-03-14 are fraud' because of one incident.

notes.front: Underfitting: what is it and how does it show up?
notes.back: The model is too simple (or under-trained) to capture the real pattern; both training and validation error are high.Example: Fitting a straight line to seasonal traffic. The model cannot represent the weekly cycle no matter how much data you give it.

notes.front: Train / validation / test split: what is each for, and what is the cardinal sin?
notes.back: Train: fit parameters. Validation: choose hyperparameters and model variants. Test: one final, untouched estimate of real-world performance. Cardinal sin: tuning on the test set—every decision made by looking at it leaks information and makes its score optimistic.Example: You try 50 model configurations and report the best test accuracy. That number is the max of 50 noisy draws, not an unbiased estimate; expect it to fall in production.

notes.front: Data leakage: what is it and what are common forms?
notes.back: Information from outside the training set (especially from the future or from the label) sneaks into features. Forms: random splits of time-series data, preprocessing (scaling, imputation) fit on all data before splitting, features that are consequences of the label, duplicates across splits.Example: A churn model with feature 'number of support tickets in the 30 days after signup' when churn is measured at day 30. Or an incident predictor trained with a 'severity' field that is only set after the incident. Suspiciously good results usually mean leakage.

notes.front: Bias–variance decomposition: state it and give the intuition.
notes.back: Expected error = bias² + variance + irreducible noise. Bias: systematic error from a model too simple to represent the truth. Variance: error from sensitivity to the particular training sample (a different sample would give a different model).Example: Archery: bias = your arrows cluster tightly but off-center (consistent, wrong); variance = arrows scattered around the bullseye (right on average, unreliable). A rule-based fraud filter has high bias; a 10,000-tree model on 500 examples has high variance.

notes.front: How do model complexity and training-set size interact with bias and variance?
notes.back: More complex model → lower bias, higher variance. More data → lower variance (complex models become safe). So the right complexity depends on how much data you have; the same architecture overfits on 1k rows and underfits on 1B.Example: Deep learning 'works' partly because web-scale data drives variance down enough to afford billion-parameter models. The same model on a small in-house dataset is a variance machine.

notes.front: Regularization: what is it, and name the main techniques.
notes.back: Any constraint that penalizes complexity to reduce variance at a small cost in bias. L2 (weight decay): shrink weights. L1: sparsify. Dropout: randomly disable units so no single one is relied upon. Data augmentation: enlarge the effective dataset. Early stopping: halt before memorization.Example: Weight decay is a prior that 'weights are probably small'; it is Bayesian MAP estimation with a Gaussian prior. Dropout is training an ensemble of thinned networks that share weights.

notes.front: Early stopping: how does it work and why is it a form of regularization?
notes.back: Track validation loss during training; stop when it starts rising even though training loss keeps falling. Fewer steps means the weights had less opportunity to drift far from initialization and fit noise.Example: Training curves: train loss ↓ smoothly, validation loss ↓ then ↑ after epoch 12. The epoch-12 checkpoint is the model you ship, not the final one.

notes.front: k-fold cross-validation: what problem does it solve?
notes.back: A single validation split gives a noisy performance estimate, especially with small data. Split into k folds, train on k−1, validate on the held-out fold, rotate, average. Uses all data for both training and validation and gives a spread, not just a point.Example: With 800 examples, a single 20% validation set is 160 examples—accuracy ±4% by chance alone. 5-fold CV averages over 5 such estimates and shows the variance between folds.

notes.front: Why must you always compare against a baseline, and what are good baselines?
notes.back: Absolute metrics are meaningless without knowing what a trivial model achieves. Baselines: predict the majority class, predict the mean, 'same as yesterday', a simple linear model, a hand-written rule.Example: 'Our outage predictor is 99.5% accurate.' Outages happen 0.4% of the time, so 'always predict no outage' is 99.6% accurate. The model is worse than nothing.

notes.front: Precision vs recall: definitions and the trade-off.
notes.back: Precision = of the things flagged, what fraction were real. Recall = of the real things, what fraction were flagged. Raising the decision threshold trades recall for precision. Which matters depends on the cost of each error type.Example: Spam filter: high precision matters (don't lose real mail). Cancer screening or intrusion detection: high recall matters (follow-up tests catch the false positives). F1 is the harmonic mean if you want one number.

notes.front: ROC curve and AUC: what are they and what is the common misuse?
notes.back: ROC plots true-positive rate vs false-positive rate across all thresholds; AUC (Area Under the Curve) is the probability the model ranks a random positive above a random negative. Misuse: on heavily imbalanced data, ROC-AUC looks great while precision is terrible; use precision–recall curves there.Example: AUC 0.95 for a fraud model with 0.1% fraud rate can still mean 50 false alarms for every real fraud caught. The ROC's false-positive axis is a fraction of a huge negative class, so small fractions hide large counts.

notes.front: Calibration: what does it mean for a probabilistic model to be calibrated, and why does it matter?
notes.back: Among all predictions of '70%', about 70% should be positive. Accuracy can be high with terrible calibration. Matters whenever the probability is used for a decision, threshold, or expected-value calculation.Example: A model says 'this deploy has a 5% rollback risk'. If historically 30% of its '5%' deploys were rolled back, the number is useless for risk budgeting. Check with a reliability diagram; fix with temperature scaling or isotonic regression.

notes.front: Distribution shift: what is it and why do models silently rot?
notes.back: Production data drifts away from training data (new users, new attack patterns, seasonal change, the model's own effect on behavior). The model's validation score was measured on the old distribution and stops applying, often with no error message.Example: A fraud model trained pre-2020 sees a pandemic-era surge of first-time online shoppers and flags them all. Or a recommender changes what users see, which changes what they click, which changes the training data—feedback loop.

notes.front: How do you avoid being fooled by an ML result in a paper or a demo? Give a checklist.
notes.back: Ask: (1) What is the baseline and is it tuned fairly? (2) Is the test set truly held out—any leakage or tuning on it? (3) Is the effect size meaningful, with variance across seeds/folds? (4) How many configurations were tried before this one? (5) Does the test distribution match where it will be used? (6) Is the metric the thing you care about?Example: 'Our model beats GPT-x by 3 points on benchmark Y.' Was Y in the training data? Was the comparison run with the same prompting effort? Is 3 points larger than seed-to-seed variance? Would the gain survive on your data?

notes.front: Double descent: what is it and why does it complicate the classical bias–variance picture?
notes.back: As model size grows, test error falls, rises near the point where the model can exactly fit the training data (interpolation threshold), then falls again in the heavily overparameterized regime. Classical theory predicted only the first rise.Example: A network with 10× more parameters than data points can generalize better than one with 1.1×. The very worst place to be is 'just barely enough capacity to memorize'. This is part of why 'bigger is better' held empirically in deep learning.

notes.front: Why does the No-Free-Lunch theorem matter in practice, and what is its practical reading?
notes.back: Averaged over all possible problems, no learning algorithm beats any other. Practical reading: every algorithm encodes assumptions (inductive bias) about what patterns are likely; it works where those assumptions hold. Choose models by matching their bias to the problem structure.Example: Convolutional networks assume nearby pixels matter together and patterns can appear anywhere; superb for images, wrong for tabular data where gradient-boosted trees, which assume axis-aligned splits, usually win.
